column1: Which OSI layer do switches primarily operate at, and what address do they use?
column2: Layer 2 (Data Link) — they forward using MAC addresses.

column1: Which OSI layer do routers operate at, and what address do they use?
column2: Layer 3 (Network) — they forward using IP addresses.

column1: Name the 7 OSI layers, top to bottom.
column2: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical. (All People Seem To Need Data Processing)

column1: What is the OSI Layer 4 PDU called? Layer 3? Layer 2?
column2: L4 = segment, L3 = packet, L2 = frame.

column1: In a three-tier campus design, what are the three layers?
column2: Access (end devices plug in), Distribution (routing + policy), Core (fast backbone).

column1: What is a "collapsed core" design?
column2: A two-tier design merging core and distribution — used when a site is too small to justify a separate core.

column1: In spine-leaf, how many hops separate any two servers?
column2: Always two (leaf → spine → leaf) — that's the point: predictable latency for east-west traffic.

column1: What does "east-west" traffic mean?
column2: Server-to-server traffic inside the data center (vs north-south = user → server → internet).

column1: What's the key difference between a VM and a container?
column2: A VM contains a full guest OS; a container shares the host kernel and holds only the app — so it's far smaller and starts in seconds.

column1: What does a VRF provide?
column2: Multiple separate routing tables on one physical router. VLANs separate at L2; VRFs separate at L3.

column1: PoE: how much power does 802.3af provide? 802.3at? 802.3bt?
column2: af ≈ 15.4 W, at (PoE+) ≈ 30 W, bt (PoE++) ≈ 60–100 W — measured at the switch port.

column1: Why is a non-PoE laptop safe to plug into a PoE port?
column2: The switch performs detection first — no powered-device signature means it sends data only.

column1: Which cable connects two switches together without Auto-MDIX?
column2: A crossover cable (like devices → crossover; unlike devices → straight-through).

column1: What is the maximum length of a copper UTP Ethernet run?
column2: 100 metres.

column1: Single-mode vs multi-mode fiber — which goes further and why?
column2: Single-mode — a narrower core carries one light path, so there's no modal dispersion; good for kilometres.

column1: TCP or UDP: which is connection-oriented and reliable?
column2: TCP — handshake, sequencing, acknowledgments, retransmission.

column1: Why does voice/video use UDP rather than TCP?
column2: A retransmitted voice packet arrives too late to be useful. Speed and steady timing matter more than perfect delivery.

column1: What are the three steps of the TCP handshake?
column2: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK.

column1: Why does closing a TCP connection normally take four messages?
column2: TCP is full duplex — each direction closes independently (FIN/ACK each way), so a half-close is legal.

column1: Do TCP sequence numbers count packets or bytes?
column2: Bytes. That's why one ACK can confirm an arbitrary amount of data.

column1: What does an ACK number actually mean?
column2: The next byte expected — so Ack=3001 means "everything below 3001 arrived."

column1: What do three duplicate ACKs trigger?
column2: Fast retransmit — resend just the missing segment without waiting for a timeout.

column1: Flow control vs congestion control — what does each protect?
column2: Flow control protects the receiver (advertised Window field); congestion control protects the network (inferred from loss).

column1: What is the typical MSS on an Ethernet network, and how is it derived?
column2: 1460 = 1500 MTU − 20 IP header − 20 TCP header.

column1: Why do tunnels (GRE/IPsec/PPPoE) cause mysterious connectivity failures?
column2: Their extra headers shrink the usable MTU; traffic sized for 1500 no longer fits and gets dropped.

column1: Port 22? Port 23?
column2: 22 = SSH, 23 = Telnet.

column1: Port 53? Ports 67/68?
column2: 53 = DNS, 67/68 = DHCP (server/client).

column1: Port 80? Port 443?
column2: 80 = HTTP, 443 = HTTPS.

column1: Ports 20/21? Port 69?
column2: 20/21 = FTP (data/control), 69 = TFTP.

column1: Port 161/162? Port 514? Port 123?
column2: 161/162 = SNMP, 514 = syslog, 123 = NTP.

column1: Port 25? Port 110?
column2: 25 = SMTP, 110 = POP3.

column1: What are the 8 binary place values in one octet?
Convert 192 to binary.
Convert binary 10101100 to decimal.
How many bits in a MAC address, and how is it split?
column2: 48 bits — first 24 = OUI (vendor), last 24 = device-specific.

column1: Write out the broadcast MAC address.
column2: FFFF.FFFF.FFFF — all 48 bits set to 1.

column1: What are the three ways to address a frame?
column2: Unicast (one), Broadcast (all), Multicast (a subscribed group).

column1: How does a switch learn MAC addresses?
column2: From the source MAC of incoming frames, mapped to the port they arrived on.

column1: What does a switch do with a frame whose destination MAC is unknown?
column2: Floods it out every port except the one it arrived on (unknown unicast flooding).

column1: Collision domain vs broadcast domain — what separates each?
column2: Each switch port is its own collision domain; each VLAN / router interface bounds a broadcast domain.

column1: What problem do VLANs solve?
column2: They split one physical switch into multiple broadcast domains, without buying more switches.

column1: Access port vs trunk port?
column2: Access carries one VLAN, untagged, to an end device. Trunk carries many VLANs, tagged, between switches.

column1: How big is an 802.1Q tag and what's the key field?
column2: 4 bytes, containing a 12-bit VLAN ID (1–4094).

column1: What is the native VLAN?
column2: The one VLAN sent untagged across a trunk. Default is VLAN 1 — best practice is to change it.

column1: What's the normal VLAN range vs the extended range?
column2: Normal 1–1005, extended 1006–4094.

column1: Why do two VLANs need a router (or SVI) to communicate?
column2: VLANs are separate broadcast domains = separate subnets, and moving between subnets is by definition Layer 3 routing.

column1: What is "router on a stick"?
column2: Inter-VLAN routing via one trunk link to a router using subinterfaces, one per VLAN.

column1: Command to put port Fa0/1 into VLAN 10?
column2: interface fa0/1 → switchport mode access → switchport access vlan 10.

column1: What are the three port-security violation modes, and which is default?
column2: protect, restrict, shutdown — shutdown is the default (err-disables the port).

column1: How do you recover an err-disabled port?
column2: shutdown then no shutdown on the interface (after fixing the cause).

column1: Why disable DTP with switchport nonegotiate?
column2: DTP can be tricked into forming a trunk with an attacker, exposing every VLAN. Set modes statically instead.

column1: What problem does STP solve?
column2: Layer 2 loops — which cause broadcast storms, MAC table instability and duplicate frames. Frames have no TTL, so a loop never self-clears.

column1: What are the default STP timers?
column2: Hello 2 s, Max Age 20 s, Forward Delay 15 s — hence ~30–50 s convergence.

column1: What is the default bridge priority, and what increments is it set in?
column2: 32768, in steps of 4096.

column1: Why must STP priority move in steps of 4096?
column2: The lower 12 bits of the priority field hold the extended system ID (the VLAN), leaving only the top 4 bits adjustable.

column1: How is the root bridge elected?
column2: Lowest Bridge ID — priority first, then lowest MAC address as tie-break.

column1: STP port costs for 10 Mbps / 100 Mbps / 1 Gbps / 10 Gbps?
When is STP root path cost added — sending or receiving?
column2: On reception — a switch adds the cost of the port the BPDU arrived on.

column1: What are STP's four tie-breakers, in order?
column2: 1) lowest Root Bridge ID, 2) lowest Root Path Cost, 3) lowest Sender Bridge ID, 4) lowest Sender Port ID.

column1: How many root ports does a non-root switch have? How many designated ports per segment?
column2: Exactly one root port per non-root switch; exactly one designated port per segment.

column1: What does PortFast do, and where is it safe?
column2: Skips listening/learning so a port forwards immediately — only on access ports facing end devices.

column1: What does BPDU Guard do?
column2: Err-disables a port that receives a BPDU — a PC port should never see one.

column1: What does Root Guard do?
column2: Prevents a switch on that port from becoming root — a superior BPDU puts the port in root-inconsistent state.

column1: What does Loop Guard protect against?
column2: A blocking port that stops receiving BPDUs (unidirectional link failure) wrongly starting to forward and creating a loop.

column1: BPDU Guard vs Loop Guard — the one-line distinction?
column2: BPDU Guard reacts to a BPDU appearing; Loop Guard reacts to BPDUs disappearing. One fears noise, the other silence.

column1: What is the default spanning-tree mode on modern Cisco switches?
column2: Rapid PVST+ — 802.1w speed with one instance per VLAN.

column1: Why run one spanning tree per VLAN?
column2: Different switches can be root for different VLANs, so both uplinks carry traffic instead of one sitting idle.

column1: What are the three RSTP port states?
column2: Discarding, Learning, Forwarding.

column1: RSTP alternate port vs backup port?
column2: Alternate = backup for the root port, hearing superior BPDUs from another switch. Backup = backup for a designated port on the same shared segment (same switch).

column1: Why is RSTP fast without timers?
column2: The proposal/agreement handshake — the neighbour blocks its own downstream ports (sync) then explicitly agrees, so safety comes from agreement rather than elapsed time.

column1: Why can a duplex mismatch cost you RSTP's fast convergence?
column2: Half duplex makes RSTP treat the link as shared rather than point-to-point, so it falls back to timers.

column1: What does EtherChannel do for STP?
column2: Makes several physical links appear as one logical link, so STP won't block the redundant members.

column1: LACP vs PAgP — which is the open standard?
column2: LACP (802.3ad) is the standard; PAgP is Cisco-proprietary.

column1: LACP modes that will form a channel?
column2: active/active or active/passive. (passive/passive will not.)

column1: Does a single file transfer go faster over a 4×1 Gbps EtherChannel?
column2: No — a flow is hashed to one link, so it's capped at 1 Gbps. EtherChannel scales many conversations.

column1: Why hash flows to a link instead of round-robining packets?
column2: Round-robin would deliver packets out of order, which TCP reads as loss — triggering retransmits and cutting throughput.

column1: Why prefer 2, 4 or 8 links in a bundle?
column2: The hash space divides evenly only across powers of two; other counts leave links permanently lopsided.

column1: What are the three private IPv4 ranges?
What does an address in 169.254.x.x mean?
column2: APIPA — the host could not reach a DHCP server and self-assigned.

column1: What is the loopback address range?
column2: 127.0.0.0/8 (usually 127.0.0.1) — tests the local TCP/IP stack.

column1: Formula for usable hosts in a subnet?
column2: 2^(host bits) − 2 (subtracting network and broadcast addresses).

column1: Formula for number of subnets when borrowing bits?
column2: 2^(borrowed bits).

column1: How many usable hosts in a /24? /26? /30?
What mask is /26, and what is its block size?
What mask is /27, and what is its block size?
What mask is /28? /29?
In 172.16.40.0/21, what is the block size and next network?
column2: /21 = 255.255.248.0 → block 8 in the third octet → next network 172.16.48.0.

column1: What is the network address of 192.168.10.77/26?
column2: Block size 64 → boundaries 0, 64, 128, 192 → network 192.168.10.64, broadcast .127.

column1: Why is a /30 used for router-to-router links?
column2: It gives exactly 2 usable addresses — one per router — wasting nothing. (/31 is also valid for p2p.)

column1: What is VLSM, and what's its golden rule?
column2: Different-sized subnets from one block. Always allocate the largest subnet first.

column1: How do you build a wildcard mask?
column2: Invert the subnet mask (255 − each octet). 0 = must match, 255 = don't care. /24 → 0.0.0.255.

column1: How long is an IPv6 address, and how long is its header?
column2: 128 bits; the header is a fixed 40 bytes.

column1: What are the two IPv6 shortening rules?
column2: Drop leading zeros in a group, and replace one run of all-zero groups with ::.

column1: What is the link-local prefix?
column2: FE80::/10 — every IPv6 interface has one, and it's never routed off the link.

column1: What prefix is unique local? Multicast?
column2: Unique local FC00::/7 (in practice FD00::/8); multicast FF00::/8.

column1: What are FF02::1 and FF02::2?
column2: All-nodes and all-routers on the link.

column1: How does EUI-64 build an interface ID from a MAC?
column2: Split the MAC, insert FFFE in the middle, and flip the 7th bit of the first byte.

column1: Does IPv6 have broadcast?
column2: No — it uses multicast (and anycast) instead.

column1: What replaced ARP in IPv6?
column2: NDP — Neighbor Solicitation / Neighbor Advertisement over ICMPv6.

column1: What are the five NDP message types?
Why does NDP use solicited-node multicast instead of broadcast?
column2: A NIC filters multicast in hardware, so uninvolved hosts' CPUs are never interrupted — unlike ARP's broadcast.

column1: What is DAD and how does it work?
column2: Duplicate Address Detection — the host sends an NS for its own tentative address; silence means it's free.

column1: What is SLAAC?
column2: Stateless Address Autoconfiguration — the host learns the prefix from an RA and generates its own host portion.

column1: What do the RA M and O flags mean?
column2: M=1 → get the address from stateful DHCPv6. O=1 → address via SLAAC but other config (DNS) from DHCPv6.

column1: Why keep DHCPv6 when SLAAC exists?
column2: SLAAC keeps no record of who holds which address — enterprises needing auditing/accountability require the central ledger.

column1: What are the Administrative Distances for connected, static, EIGRP, OSPF and RIP?
column2: 0, 1, 90, 110, 120. (255 = untrusted/never used.)

column1: What does Administrative Distance decide?
column2: Which source to believe when several describe the same network. Lower = more trusted.

column1: What does a metric decide, and how does it differ from AD?
column2: Metric picks the best path within one protocol. AD picks which protocol/source to trust first.

column1: What is longest prefix match?
column2: The router uses the most specific matching route — /30 beats /24 beats /8 — regardless of AD or metric.

column1: What is a floating static route?
column2: A static route with a deliberately raised AD, so it only takes over if the preferred route disappears.

column1: Syntax for a default route?
column2: ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 <next-hop> — the "everywhere else" route.

column1: What problem does an FHRP solve?
column2: A host's default gateway is a single static setting — hosts can't switch on their own, so the routers must share one virtual IP.

column1: Why must an FHRP share a virtual MAC, not just a virtual IP?
column2: Hosts address frames to the cached MAC; moving only the IP would leave them sending to a dead router until ARP caches expired.

column1: HSRP vs VRRP vs GLBP?
column2: HSRP Cisco, Active/Standby. VRRP open standard, Master/Backup. GLBP Cisco, also load balances.

column1: How does HSRP elect the active router?
column2: Highest priority (default 100); tie broken by highest IP address.

column1: What does standby 1 preempt do, and where must it be configured?
column2: Lets a recovered router reclaim Active. It's needed on the router with the higher priority.

column1: HSRP default hello and hold timers?
column2: Hello 3 s, hold 10 s.

column1: What type of routing protocol is OSPF, and what algorithm does it run?
column2: Link-state, running Dijkstra's SPF over its database.

column1: OSPF hello and dead intervals on broadcast/p2p links?
column2: Hello 10 s, Dead 40 s.

column1: How is the OSPF Router ID chosen?
column2: Manual router-id first; else the highest loopback IP; else the highest active physical interface IP.

column1: How is OSPF cost calculated, and what's the default reference bandwidth?
column2: Reference bandwidth ÷ interface bandwidth; default reference is 100 Mbps (so anything ≥100 Mbps computes to 1).

column1: What must match for OSPF neighbors to form?
column2: Area ID, hello/dead timers, subnet/mask, authentication, MTU, and compatible network type. (Router IDs must be unique, not matching.)

column1: Why does OSPF elect a DR and BDR on broadcast segments?
column2: To cut adjacencies from n(n−1)/2 to a hub-and-spoke around the DR, avoiding duplicate flooding.

column1: How is the OSPF DR elected?
column2: Highest interface priority (default 1), tie broken by highest Router ID. Priority 0 = never eligible.

column1: Is the OSPF DR election preemptive?
column2: No — a new higher-priority router does not take over an existing DR. (Contrast: HSRP with preempt does.)

column1: Is 2WAY/DROTHER in show ip ospf neighbor a problem?
column2: No — two DROTHERs deliberately stop at 2WAY. They only go FULL with the DR and BDR.

column1: Which command skips the DR/BDR election on a 2-router link?
column2: ip ospf network point-to-point.

column1: What are the OSPF neighbor states in order?
column2: Down → Init → 2-Way → ExStart → Exchange → Loading → Full.

column1: An adjacency stuck in EXSTART/EXCHANGE usually means what?
column2: An MTU mismatch — hellos are small enough to pass, but the larger DBD packets are dropped.

column1: What does "Init" state indicate?
column2: One-way communication — you hear their hello but aren't listed in it (often an ACL or mask problem).

column1: OSPF LSA Type 1 and Type 2 — what are they?
column2: Type 1 = Router LSA (a router's own links). Type 2 = Network LSA, generated by the DR to describe a broadcast segment.

column1: OSPF LSA Types 3 and 5?
column2: Type 3 = Summary (inter-area, from the ABR). Type 5 = External (redistributed, from the ASBR).

column1: What does a stub area block, and what does it get instead?
column2: Blocks Type 5 externals; receives a default route instead.

column1: Why must every router in an OSPF area hold an identical database?
column2: Each computes its own tree from it — identical input + deterministic algorithm = consistent, loop-free forwarding.

column1: What are the four DHCP steps?
column2: DORA — Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.

column1: Why is ip helper-address needed?
column2: DHCP Discover is a broadcast, and routers don't forward broadcasts — the helper relays it as unicast to the server.

column1: What does DNS do, and on which port?
column2: Resolves names to IP addresses, on port 53.

column1: Pinging an IP works but pinging a hostname fails. What does that isolate, and why?
column2: DNS. Reaching the IP proves routing and the gateway are fine, so only name resolution is left.

column1: Static NAT vs dynamic NAT vs PAT?
column2: Static = permanent 1-to-1. Dynamic = from a pool, as needed. PAT/overload = many hosts share one IP using ports.

column1: Which NAT type lets an outside host initiate a connection inward, and why?
column2: Static NAT — the mapping is permanent and bidirectional; PAT entries only exist after an inside host starts a conversation.

column1: What keyword turns NAT into PAT?
column2: overload — as in ip nat inside source list 1 interface gi0/1 overload.

column1: Which command shows the live NAT table?
column2: show ip nat translations.

column1: Why does NTP matter for security?
column2: Logs, certificates and authentication all depend on accurate time; skewed clocks break correlation and validation.

column1: Syslog severity levels 0–7?
column2: 0 Emergency, 1 Alert, 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notification, 6 Informational, 7 Debugging. (Lower = more severe.)

column1: SNMP: what's a get vs a trap?
column2: A get is the manager polling the device; a trap is the device pushing an alert unprompted.

column1: Which QoS marking is used for voice?
column2: EF — Expedited Forwarding, DSCP 46.

column1: Policing vs shaping?
column2: Policing drops excess traffic; shaping buffers it to send later.

column1: What is jitter, and what's the target for voice?
column2: Variation in delay — under 30 ms. (One-way delay under 150 ms, loss under 1%.)

column1: What is a QoS trust boundary?
column2: The point where the network decides whether to believe incoming markings — you trust an IP phone, not a user's PC.

column1: What are the three parts of the CIA triad?
column2: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability.

column1: What's at the end of every ACL, even unwritten?
column2: An implicit deny any.

column1: How are ACL entries processed?
column2: Top down, first match wins — and processing stops there.

column1: Where do you place a standard ACL vs an extended ACL, and why?
column2: Standard near the destination (it only matches source, so placing it early would over-block); extended near the source (it's specific, so drop unwanted traffic early).

column1: What can a standard ACL match? An extended ACL?
column2: Standard: source IP only. Extended: source + destination IP, protocol and ports.

column1: What are the three AAA functions?
column2: Authentication (who are you), Authorization (what may you do), Accounting (what did you do).

column1: RADIUS vs TACACS+ — key differences?
column2: RADIUS: UDP, encrypts only the password, combines authn+authz. TACACS+: TCP, encrypts the entire payload, separates all three functions.

column1: What does DHCP snooping prevent?
column2: A rogue DHCP server — untrusted ports aren't allowed to send DHCP offers.

column1: What does Dynamic ARP Inspection prevent, and what does it rely on?
column2: ARP poisoning / man-in-the-middle — it validates ARP against the DHCP snooping binding table.

column1: What is 802.1X, and what are the three roles?
column2: Port-based authentication before network access. Supplicant (client), Authenticator (switch), Authentication server (RADIUS).

column1: What makes authentication truly multi-factor?
column2: Two different factor types — know / have / are. A password + security question is not MFA.

column1: Why are biometrics risky as a sole credential?
column2: You can't change them. A leaked password is replaced in seconds; a leaked fingerprint is compromised permanently.

column1: Why does physical access control belong in network security?
column2: Physical access defeats most software controls — console access allows password recovery, and any port can be used.

column1: Which 2.4 GHz channels are non-overlapping?
Why does 5 GHz generally outperform 2.4 GHz?
column2: More non-overlapping channels and less interference — at the cost of shorter range and weaker wall penetration.

column1: What is an SSID?
column2: The wireless network name clients see and join.

column1: What is the wireless access method, and why not CSMA/CD?
column2: CSMA/CA (collision avoidance) — radios can't transmit and listen simultaneously, so collisions can't be detected, only avoided.

column1: WPA2 vs WPA3 — what's the main encryption/authentication difference?
column2: WPA2 uses AES-CCMP with a 4-way handshake; WPA3 adds SAE ("Dragonfly"), resisting offline dictionary attacks.

column1: Autonomous AP vs lightweight AP?
column2: Autonomous = self-contained, configured individually. Lightweight = managed by a WLC, via CAPWAP.

column1: Which 802.11 standard is Wi-Fi 6, and which bands does it use?
column2: 802.11ax — both 2.4 and 5 GHz (6 GHz with 6E).

column1: What are the two planes SDN separates?
column2: Control plane (decides where traffic goes) and data plane (actually forwards it).

column1: Northbound vs southbound API?
column2: Northbound faces apps/users (controller ↔ your scripts). Southbound faces the devices (controller ↔ switches).

column1: What does CRUD map to in REST?
column2: Create=POST, Read=GET, Update=PUT/PATCH, Delete=DELETE.

column1: What does a 401 mean? A 404? A 500?
column2: 401 not authenticated, 404 not found, 500 server error. 4xx = your mistake, 5xx = the server's.

column1: What does it mean that REST is stateless?
column2: Every request carries everything needed to answer it — the server remembers nothing between calls, which is what makes it scalable.

column1: What are the JSON data types?
column2: String, number, boolean, null, array [], object {}.

column1: Ansible vs Terraform vs Puppet — which need agents?
column2: Ansible and Terraform are agentless; Puppet/Chef require an agent on each node.

column1: Declarative vs procedural configuration?
column2: Declarative describes the desired end state and the tool computes the change; procedural lists the steps to run in order.

column1: What is idempotence?
column2: Applying the same change repeatedly produces the same result — running it ten times is as safe as once.

column1: How does ML-based monitoring improve on fixed thresholds?
column2: It learns a baseline of normal for that network and flags deviations — catching gradual degradation that never crosses a static limit.

column1: Which commands show IP settings on Windows, macOS and Linux?
column2: ipconfig /all (Windows), ifconfig (macOS), ip address (Linux).

column1: What's the trace command on Windows vs everywhere else?
column2: tracert on Windows; traceroute on macOS/Linux/IOS.

column1: How does traceroute actually discover the path?
column2: It sends packets with increasing TTL — each hop that hits TTL 0 returns an ICMP "time exceeded," revealing itself.

column1: Why does a router decrement TTL?
column2: Loop insurance — a misrouted packet dies instead of circulating forever.

column1: In a frame crossing a router, what changes and what stays the same?
column2: MAC addresses are rewritten every hop; IP addresses stay the same end to end (unless NAT intervenes).

column1: Why does a PC ARP for its gateway rather than the remote destination?
column2: Only devices on the same segment can answer ARP — the remote host isn't there to reply.

column1: A port shows "administratively down". What's the fix?
column2: no shutdown on the interface.

column1: What symptoms indicate a duplex mismatch?
column2: Slowness with late collisions on the half-duplex side and FCS/runt errors on the other.

column1: Which command shows what's connected to a Cisco device?
column2: show cdp neighbors (or show lldp neighbors for the open standard).

column1: First four things to read from ipconfig /all?
column2: IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, DNS servers — most faults show up in one of these.
